frontmatter.title: Quantum optimization
frontmatter.description: QAOA, VQE, and digitized adiabatic optimization, with explicit circuits, complete workloads, and classical C4 reference coverage.

children.value: Optimization asks for a useful classical answer: a good assignment, an energy estimate, or a verified solution. For

children.html: nnn

children.value: assignments. Quantum algorithms prepare amplitudes over candidates and change them through objective-dependent phases, interference, or Hamiltonian evolution. Measurement still returns a limited classical result. Input construction, state preparation, output quality, repetitions, and classical control therefore determine whether a proposed improvement is meaningful.
This chapter checks transparent small circuits for three approaches and adds an
executed fixed DQI circuit and public companion
. QAOA and VQE use a classical parameter search; a digitized anneal follows a prescribed Hamiltonian path. The original algorithm papers provide the theoretical context
. The implementations, exposition, and figures here are original.

The demonstrations are executed ideal numerical checks with independent classical references and downloadable circuits. Sample counts are generated classically from circuit probabilities, rather than measured on a QPU. Small results and parameterized generators do not establish large-instance convergence or quantum advantage.
Fault-tolerant reports are conditional resource models.

The reproduced Lean artifact checks finite cut values and the stated classical equality predicate; its coverage excludes QAOA and annealing correctness and physical estimates. These distinctions remain explicit below.
Alternate phases from a classical objective with a mixer; fit layer angles.
Four-vertex MaxCut, exact enumeration, and separate exact/sampled optimizer records.
Prepare a parameterized ansatz and reduce its measured energy.
A stated two-qubit Hamiltonian, exact diagonalization, and covariance-aware grouped readout.
Change an easy driver Hamiltonian into a problem Hamiltonian; digitize the evolution.
A fixed C4 path, numerical continuous reference, and separate time/slice studies.
Coherently decode a low-weight syndrome state, then Fourier-transform it into an objective-biased distribution.
Nine-wire default circuit and ordinary saved-artifact notebook executed. Larger families and physical estimates remain planned.

An expected cut, a probability of obtaining a maximum cut, and an energy error are different outputs. A fair comparison fixes the problem, required quality, confidence, and physical assumptions. The small cases below demonstrate behavior; they are not interchangeable benchmarks.

Measured local CPU controller/reference timings remain separate from modeled quantum time. Actual synthesis sequences, reset models, hardware feedback and general optimizer/quality guarantees remain outside this conditional report. Missed-quality runs cannot establish a matched-quality improvement.

Serial time is repetition-weighted and peak footprint is the maximum selected footprint. CPU control, physical reset, communication, feedback, routing, and reconfiguration overhead are excluded where unmeasured. Independently selected model points do not certify one common physical layout. Reports expose these assumptions and preserve the
; different tasks do not establish a co-design improvement at matched output quality.

Numerical coverage includes classical enumeration and scalar expectation formulas for QAOA, dense Hamiltonian eigenvalues for VQE, gate-versus-dense Strang checks and a continuous numerical reference for annealing. Export/lowering checks compare the implemented circuits up to global phase with measurement maps retained. Finite-shot bounds apply to fresh fixed-state estimates and remain separate from optimizer success and physical faults. The size study additionally checks all graph optima by enumeration, all chain ground energies by dense diagonalization, selected-state circuits against independent references, and every measured-decision trace from its counts. Its simultaneous 84-group holdout bounds do not cover adaptive training queries or extend the classical C4 proof.
